updateCadence: Irregular: 3.9 in Jul 2019, 3.10 in May 2020, 3.11 in Dec 2023
summary: A small, fast, free browser written in C with its own HTML/CSS engine and Duktape JavaScript. It runs on RISC OS, Amiga, Haiku and Linux, but handles only older web standards, so many modern sites fail.
bestFor: Retro and niche systems (RISC OS, AmigaOS, Haiku, Atari)
Very low-spec machines that cannot run a mainstream browser
Reading static, standards-based pages with minimal resource use
notFor: Anyone who needs modern web apps, video or heavy JavaScript
People who want extensions, sync or a password manager
Users who need strong security hardening or fast patches

pros.title: Very small and quick
pros.detail: Its own engine in C: the RISC OS build is 4.0 MB and the AmigaOS build 6.9 MB (per Wikipedia).

pros.title: Runs where others do not
pros.detail: Official ports for RISC OS, AmigaOS 4, Haiku/BeOS, Atari, Linux and Windows; third-party ports to MorphOS, Plan 9 and more.

pros.title: Own standards stack
pros.detail: Hubbub HTML5 parser, LibCSS, LibDOM and Duktape JavaScript, with CSS flex added in 3.11.

pros.title: No telemetry
pros.detail: A volunteer project with no business model and no data-collection service.

pros.title: Still receiving commits
pros.detail: The git mirror shows daily commits in late October 2026, including HSTS test work.

cons.title: Weak modern-web support
cons.detail: Targets HTML 4.01 and CSS 2.1 plus selected newer features; JavaScript is limited, so web apps usually fail.

cons.title: No media or web apps
cons.detail: Renders images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, SVG, WebP, JPEG XL) but not modern video or canvas-style apps.

cons.title: Thin security model
cons.detail: C codebase without sandboxing or site isolation; fixes depend on volunteers.

cons.title: Slow releases, no polished Windows build
cons.detail: Stable releases are years apart, and there is no complete native Windows port (the GTK front end is built for Windows).

faq.a: Yes, in a limited form via the Duktape engine (since 2015), but coverage is far below mainstream browsers; the project does not publish a compatibility level.
Yes, slowly. The latest stable release is 3.11 (28 Dec 2023), and the git mirror had commits on 28 Oct 2026.

faq.q: Why does my favourite site not work?
faq.a: NetSurf implements HTML 4.01 and CSS 2.1 plus newer pieces like flexbox and media queries; sites built on heavy JavaScript frameworks are out of reach.

switching.note: No importers from other browsers; bookmarks live in NetSurf's own list, so copy URLs over manually.

spec.codecs: Images only (PNG, GIF, JPEG, BMP, SVG, WebP, JPEG XL); no HTML5 media found

pageLoad: Fast on simple pages, fails on heavy ones
networkSpeed: libcurl-based fetching, no modern HTTP tuning shown
startup: Fast startup is a stated goal
memory: Small footprint is a stated goal
battery: Low CPU use on simple pages
lowEnd: Targets RISC OS, Amiga and other low-end systems
privacyDefaults: No telemetry, little scripting; no blocking
blocking: No filter lists; limited JS means fewer trackers
fingerprinting: Small surface but rare, identifiable user agent
securityHardening: No sandbox, C code, volunteer testing
webCompat: HTML 4.01, CSS 2.1 plus flex; limited JS
longevity: 24 years old and still committing, but slow releases
beginnerFriendly: Simple GUI, but sites often fail
